 STANDARD ACTIONS [ Backing chit unless otherwise specified]
- Propose a partial translation by playing a Gloss Card. If playing as your Character, play Gloss Card face-down on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Character Card. If playing as your Academic, play this card face up on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Academic card or any Voting Rules card in play.
- You may propose an Alternate Manuscript language using a Language Card in your hand. This triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote among all players with face-up Academic cards, according to the Voting Rules in play. Turn Gloss cards in the Manuscript common pool face down except those matching your proposed Manuscript Language. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card.
- Propose a Crazy Idea Manuscript Language. You may also propose a novel suggestion for the Manuscript Language without playing a Language Card by spending  Backing chits.
- Propose a partial transliteration Play a Glyph card on any Voynichese card in the Manuscript common pool. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card.
- Play a card that changes the Voting Rules. Follow the instructions in the text printed on the card.
- Flip your Character  Academic Card to change the play of your turn.
- Spend  Backing chits to flip your Character  Academic Card and change the play at any time during your turn.
- Contribute to the Manuscript lore by playing legend cards according to the rules on the card.
- Preserve one clue under a Preservation card in your Cache.
UPKEEP
 - At the end of each turn, you must flip your Character  Academic card according to the instructions printed on it.
         
Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round.
         
Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round.
Voting
If you call a vote and your translation achieves Consensus, then you may take an extra turn [or draw an extra card?]. If Consensus fails, you lose your next turn [or discard?].
         
The Author Card Each character has a corresponding Author Card. At the begining of a vote, the player who announces the vote draws a card. If you draw your author card, then you are the author of the manuscript, and you must look through the deck, removing all other Author cards from the deck. If any other card is drawn, you must look through the deck and choose seven(or whatever the number of characters is) cards of your choosing and place them face down in front of you. You may choose any cards in the deck, including any Author cards. These cards may not be used until the Final Round, in which they will replace your hand. You may not reveal the cards, nor whether or not you are the author (except by preserving evidence) until the end of the game. If you are the Author of the Manuscript, then begining with this vote, you MUST choose either to conceal your authorship by only voting against any Translation that indicates your authorship [e.g. votes that include any of Language(s) or Locality] or you must choose not to conceal your authorship by voting for any Translation that indicates your authorship. Once you have chosen whether or not to conceal your authorship, you may ONLY vote in accordance with this choice, you may not alternate. In either case, you may not reveal whether you are the author or not until the end of the game, except by preserving evidence.

A player gives clues that they want some, but not all, players to guess.


         

Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects andor have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.


         
Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects andor have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. In storytelling games, players are provided with conceptual, written, or pictorial stimuli which must be incorporated into a story of the players' creation. Once Upon a Time uses a selection of words while Rory's Story Cubes include ambiguous symbols. Some games like Snake Oil and Big Idea  players to pitch a product, which frequently takes the form of a brief story or vignette.

Other storytelling games include titles such as Tales of the Arabian Nights and Above and Below, game designs in which players don't create their own stories, but instead experience a story from the inside as one of the participants. Games along those lines might present players with a particular narrative situation, after which the player will make a choice that affects which end to the narrative is told with the results of this narrative affecting the player's standing in the game.


         
A game in which players are cooperating and competing with each other throughout the game, while trying to complete a common objective. To be classified as semi-cooperative, there must be two possible end states

A) One or more (but unlikely to be all) players win
B) No players win

A game where players sometimes cooperate and sometimes compete but one always wins is not semi-cooperative. It is a Competitive game with a Negotiation mechanism.


         
Secret unit deployment games are games that contain hidden information. Only the player controlling certain playing pieces has perfect information about the nature (or even the whereabouts) of those pieces. This mechanic is often used in wargames to simulate "fog of war".


         
A game system that can be applied to a variety of different maps, starting resources and positions, and even different win and loss conditions. These variable conditions can be assembled into a broader narrative or campaign, or they can be entirely disconnected from one another.


         
Some board games incorporate elements of role playing. It can be that players control a character that improves over time. It can also be a game that encourages or inspires Storytelling. This mechanic can be viewed as an extension of Variable Player Powers.


         
Resources are ed from a random process and distributed to qualifying players.


         
Players ask and answer questions in a manner constrained by rules.


         
The Pieces themselves compose the Map.

This is distinct from Tile Placement in that the map elements remain “pieces” after placement, and accordingly continue to have agency in the game mechanics.


         
Pieces are removed from a structure, and play is affected by things that fall (as in Ker Plunk), or a complete collapse of the structure (as in Jenga).


         
Players possess one or more Action Tokens. Those who have an Action Token may take a turn, then they pass the token clockwise, allowing the next player to perform an action. Actions are performed in real time; - there is no pausing and structure within the turn.

Typically, to prevent stalling and to keep the game moving, in games with multiple Action Tokens, if both tokens are held by the same player, then they suffer a penalty.


         
Players have a special ability that they can use one time per game.

These may be unique to them, like 'feats' in Warmachine, or common to all players, like the special power chits in Finca.

Often players will receive bonus Victory Points if they do not use their one-time abilities during the game.


         
Actions, resources, or resolution are shared between neighbors.


         
Multiple action options are presented to the players via a narrative format.

These can be presented in a book with numbered paragraphs as in Tales of the Arabian Nights or Above and Below, or via cards as in Dead of Winter A Crossroads Game.


         
Multiple actions are shown on a card, but only one can be used.


         
Players Move Through a Deck of cards. Typically the goal is to reach the bottom (One Deck Dungeon), find and defeat a boss (Chainsaw Warrior), or simply know when to quit (Diamant).


         
When a conflict is initiated, pieces are moved to a separate board for resolution.


         
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.

Rummy games have players placing combinations of cards or tiles on the table to score. Innovation is a good example of the Splaying side, where players can spread cards out to show particular sets of icons to empower abilities.


         
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.


         
Players must make their next play by matching a feature on the previous play. This is frequently used in shedding games like UNO or Crazy Eights, where number or colorsuit need to be matched.

In some implementations the next play needs to be in a number range based on the last. For example, in L.L.A.M.A. the play must be the same or one higher than the last. In Spit, it must be one higher or lower.

NOTE Although this is similar to 'following suit' in a trick taking game, or 'ladder climbing' games, please use those mechanisms instead.


         
Over the course of the game, the map shrinks.


         
A multi-session game in which permanent and irreversible changes to the game state carry over to future plays. Components may be written on with permanent ink, torn apart, covered with a sticker, etc.


         
Players contribute towards completing a task, but only the player who finally completes it gets a particular benefit or bonus reward (even if others share in the base level benefit).


         
This is a meta-mechanic for Turn Order. Players may take an action that interrupts the normal turn flow.


         
The number of Victory Points held by each player is private information.


         
Movement occurs that is not visible to all players.

Scotland Yard is a classic game implementing this mechanism.

A key challenge for designers is determining how to make the movement rules simple enough that the players moving hidden units do not make mistakes, or that paths are traceable when the game concludes.


         
Hand management games are games with cards in them that reward players for playing the cards in certain sequences or groups. The optimal sequencegrouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.

Hand management has no relationship to actiondexterity.

The optimal sequencegrouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.


         
When the main game ends, a special mini-game is played to determine the victor.


         
Different Dice are used to move depending on unit or game state.


         
"Dice Rolling" is a game mechanism that can be used for many things, randomness being the most obvious.

In wargames, "Dice Rolling" is used in conjunction with a variety of tables, notably a "Combat Results Table" (either as a Ratio or a Differential) which produces a result by strengths of both sides and a die roll (D, D, and D are most commonly used).


         
Players are trying to determine the identity of hidden information based on clues.
         
Dice are rolled, and those exceeding a target number e a success. Certain rolls (typically the highest andor lowest on the die) e additional success or extreme failure.


         
Players coordinate their actions to achieve a common win condition or conditions. Players all win or lose the game together.


         
Games may limit players from communicating with one another openly. These restrictions can be absolute as they relate to certain specific pieces of information, or they may restrict certain types of communication, such as speaking.

Examples of this mechanism include Hanabi and Reverse Charades.


         
Players have a hand of cards that allows them to activate and perform actions with a subset of their units.


         
Closed Drafting (or 'Card Drafting') is a means of distributing cards or other game elements to players through an ordered, closed selection process - typically "select and pass".

A typical implementation involves each player being dealt the same number of cards. Players then select one (or more) card(s) to keep, and pass the rest to their left. This continues until all cards are selected or discarded.  Wonders implements this type of draft.

An alternative is that only one player is dealt cards, and they take one and pass it until all players have cards. This obviously is strongly biased towards the first player, and needs to be supported thematically and balance-wise. Citadels implements this type of draft.

This is distinct from Open Drafting, with involves selection from a public display.


         
Pieces are stationary but are built out in chains. This can give a dynamic sense of motion to the game, even though the pieces do not move.

Early examples of this mechanism can be found in Expedition and Through the Desert.


         
Each player simultaneously or sequentially plays one or more cards. These modify the base outcome of a conflict and allow various special abilities to apply.

This can function similarly to Area Majority  Influence, but with a discrete resolution or award of the conflict target, rather than by dynamicshifting control of a fixed asset. It is also similar to Force Commitment, but that mechanic presupposes a more liquid resource where the quantity can be chosen.


         
Each player has a set of Actions available to them, embodied in cards, tokens, or some other affordance. Once performed, they are spent and may not be performed again until retrieved. Action Retrieval typically is itself an Action, or may take an entire turn.


         
The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train ().
         
A player receives a number of Action Points or Operation Points on their turn. They may spend them on a variety of Actions.

The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train ().

Economic games encourage players to manage a system of production, distribution, trade, andor consumption of goods. The games usually simulate a market in some way. The term is often used interchangeably with resource management games.


         
A strategy game is a game in which the players' decision-making skills have a high significance in determining the outcome. Strategy games often require decision tree analysis, or probabilistic estimation in the case of games with chance elements. Strategy games include abstract games, with artificial rules and little or no theme, and simulations (including wargames), with rules designed to emulate and reproduce a real or fictional scenario.

Greetings and salutations! Welcome to the third installment of the floating liars'club. Things are progressing well, although we are all extraordinarily busy. Between writing, editing, and workshopping stories, and doing layout, artwork, marketing, and promotion for the magazine, we are left little time to eat or sleep. We have received a lot of positive feedback from our readers, and the submissions have started to flow in, including interest from as far away as the U.K. We encourage anyone interested in writing to submit a piece of work. While we cannot publish everything we read, we will certainly provide feedback to anyone who requests it. While we are primarily interested in short fiction, we are also willing to look at poetry, creative nonfiction, and artwork. Submit! This issue again features the fantastic artwork and illustration of Joe Bellomy, highlighting an interesting array of stories. While we have no intention of theme from issue to issue, this month's stories seem to congeal together nicely. Many of the stories contain the theme of discovery or uncovering things, either in the figurative sense of characters uncovering things about themselves, as in Ben Crites "The Nature of Fireflies," or in the very literal sense as in my own story, "A Buried Mystery." The process of writing is one of constant uncovering and discovery. Both of the stories I included in this issue were inspired by short stories I had recently discovered, namely Jorge Luis Borges' "A Secret Miracle" and J.G. Ballard's "The Drowned Giant." This process of discovery and uncovering comes from everywhere, inside and out. Part of the process of learning to be a writer is being aware of the things you are uncovering daily. So sit back in a comfortable place with good lighting, preferably a chair, you wouldn't want to fall asleep in bed, although that's always a nice place to read, isn't it? Make sure you have something to drink at hand. Ahh, that's nice, isn't it? Now turn the page and uncover what we have wrought. It may show me I’m wrong, or show me that the person I’m talking to isn’t what I thihtt, but it always teaches me something about the person, for better or Wortes. And that helps me to learn, about them, but also sometimes I find seeing their approach gives me new ideas about my own My goal isn’t to be conciliatory by default. My goal is to check my own assumptions. I know from experience, when I’ve taken the time to listen to and try to understand why someone did something I didn’t like, usually their reasons aren’t the reasons I thought. Having an open minded discussion giving the benefit of the doubt doesn’t always convince me that the truth is somewhere in between their version and mine, but often it is, and often it’s something else altogether that I didn’t expect. And even if talking about it verifies my worst expectations or makes me realize the issue even worse than my expectations, there’s usually also other factors that mitigate or change how I feel about the thing and how I should react to it. All those acronyms, symbols, and numbers are meaningless to the average car owner. So let’s walk through each of them and explain em.


DTC P – This is the diagnostic trouble code, DTC, or Generic OBD Trouble Code
Fuel SYS CL – the fuel injector in bank  is in closed-loop mode when the error occurred.
Fuel SYS NA – means there is no fuel injector in bank . This also means the engine is either a four or six-cylinder with just a single bank.
Load PCT  – the air volume or amount of air entering the motor that is below %.
ECT  – is the Engine Coolant Temperature. In this case, the coolant temperature is  degrees F.
SHrtFT . – means the short-term fuel trim is at .%. (read more about short and long term fuel trim and live OBD data)
Long FT -. – the oxygen sensor or O sensor has not switched yet to long-term fuel trim for the fuel injectors.
Map kpa . – is the reading in the manifold absolute pressure sensor or MAP when the error occurred. In this case, the sensor has a pressure signal of . kilopascals.
VSS  – is the speed of the vehicle when the DTC occurred.
Rpm  – is the engine revolutions per minute as the error occurred.
IAT  – Intake Air Temperature is at  degrees F when the PCM detected the diagnostic trouble code.

Fresh Basil Pesto
PREP TIME
 mins
TOTAL TIME
 mins
SERVINGS
 servings
YIELD
 cup
Basil pesto darkens when exposed to air. To store, cover tightly with plastic wrap, making sure the plastic is touching the top of the pesto and not allowing the pesto to have contact with air. The pesto sauce will stay greener longer that way.
Ingredients
 cups fresh basil leaves, packed (can sub half the basil leaves with baby spinach)
 cup freshly grated Romano or Parmesan cheese (about  ounces)
 cup extra virgin olive oil
 cup pine nuts (can sub chopped walnuts)
 cloves garlic, minced (about  tablespoon)
 teaspoon salt, or more to taste
 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or more to taste

A Tealeaf
from the
Tangledays

I hope the reader will forgive this too-lengthy introduction to an all-too-brief account, but in this researcher’s belief, it is important to understand the historical context wherever possible, (all the more, given the Great Civilizations’ rather less than stellar record-keeping ethos), especially in regards to the sharp insight this unknown pupil provides into the practices and internal dynamics of the early Keeper Creches, as led by the now near-mythic Master Esthen of the Great School of Pisthen-Da. This short account was, according to its own statement, recorded by a young Keeper in training (One wonders what eventually became of this young man A dropout farm laborer, perhaps? A pioneering Keeper-Sojourner in the early centuries of the Centerward Outer Settlement Patch? Or maybe he was destined to become none other than the Great Sugh-Lehonur himself?).

Found written in a common cypher of its region, upon the Queen Leaf a great old mangroak, presumably left in situ after inscription, only to be harvested and lost among the gathered leaves of that year, it is by providence that this single tealeaf was retained for production rather than sloughed off into the chaff as tough old Queen Leaves tend to be.

The writing on the leaf survived, apparently unnoticed, throughout the processes of picking and bailing, airing and sunning, spreading and aging, heaping and fermenting, pressing and kilning, and was ultimately compressed into a brick of airy golden triss-tea and stored at a certain “Warehouse a” of an unknown farm conglomerate until that facility was incorporated into the fabled Ennbrook Exchange, whereafter it was transferred to a distribution node far out on the fringe of the Eenay Sai, where it sat unmolested for an estimated eighteen decades, before being acquired in a liquidation lot upon dissolution of the Ennbrook Exchange towards the end of the Third Age. Its chain of custody is not recorded throughout the Fourth Age, but it is thought to have gathered dust in one of the mercantile district hovels for a terribly long time before being purchased and assessed and auctioned at Mistentak on rd Merai, Year  of the Fifth Age, to one Sr. Purchaser Ms. Sensan Too who, recognizing its great age (apparently perserved in part due to the arid climes of that region), ly brewed it into a cauldron of simple light triss, which she served at a reception on th Terku of that year. The recipient of this particular leaf was a minor Abbot of the House of ChuurrTenn-U who, upon his first sip, read the unfolding cypher leaf aloud to the gathered guestsaccompanying documentation confirms a hush fell over the crowd during the first four words of the brief narrative, transcribed below

assistant esthen lectured us

about mangoak roosts [SIC] for three hours today!

If she spent that much time shoveling shit at oons-[ILLEGIBLE]

like the freshmen keepers have to,

she’d have been dean of the creche by now.

tolshe[ILLEGIBLE] put an [ILLEGIBLE] in her drinking vessel.

who’s shoveling shit now?

Fresh Basil Pesto
PREP TIME
 mins
TOTAL TIME
 mins
SERVINGS
 servings
YIELD
 cup
Basil pesto darkens when exposed to air. To store, cover tightly with plastic wrap, making sure the plastic is touching the top of the pesto and not allowing the pesto to have contact with air. The pesto sauce will stay greener longer that way.
Ingredients
 cups fresh basil leaves, packed (can sub half the basil leaves with baby spinach)
 cup freshly grated Romano or Parmesan cheese (about  ounces)
 cup extra virgin olive oil
 cup pine nuts (can sub chopped walnuts)
 cloves garlic, minced (about  tablespoon)
 teaspoon salt, or more to taste
 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or more to taste

P cylinder  injector circuit low
DTC P
Fuel SYS CL
Fuel SYS NA
….continued…
All those acronyms, symbols, and numbers are meaningless to the average car owner. So let’s walk through each of them and explain em.


DTC P – This is the diagnostic trouble code, DTC, or Generic OBD Trouble Code
Fuel SYS CL – the fuel injector in bank  is in closed-loop mode when the error occurred.
Fuel SYS NA – means there is no fuel injector in bank . This also means the engine is either a four or six-cylinder with just a single bank.
Load PCT  – the air volume or amount of air entering the motor that is below %.
ECT  – is the Engine Coolant Temperature. In this case, the coolant temperature is  degrees F.
SHrtFT . – means the short-term fuel trim is at .%. (read more about short and long term fuel trim and live OBD data)
Long FT -. – the oxygen sensor or O sensor has not switched yet to long-term fuel trim for the fuel injectors.
Map kpa . – is the reading in the manifold absolute pressure sensor or MAP when the error occurred. In this case, the sensor has a pressure signal of . kilopascals.
VSS  – is the speed of the vehicle when the DTC occurred.
Rpm  – is the engine revolutions per minute as the error occurred.
IAT  – Intake Air Temperature is at  degrees F when the PCM detected the diagnostic trouble code.

- Propose a partial translation by playing a Gloss Card. If playing as your Character, play Gloss Card face-down on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Character Card. If playing as your Academic, play this card face up on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Academic card or any Voting Rules card in play.
- You may propose an Alternate Manuscript language using a Language Card in your hand. This triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote among all players with face-up Academic cards, according to the Voting Rules in play. Turn Gloss cards in the Manuscript common pool face down except those matching your proposed Manuscript Language. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card.
- Propose a Crazy Idea Manuscript Language. You may also propose a novel suggestion for the Manuscript Language without playing a Language Card by spending  Backing chits.
- Propose a partial transliteration Play a Glyph card on any Voynichese card in the Manuscript common pool. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card.
- Play a card that changes the Voting Rules. Follow the instructions in the text printed on the card.
- Flip your Character  Academic Card to change the play of your turn.
- Spend  Backing chits to flip your Character  Academic Card and change the play at any time during your turn.
- Contribute to the Manuscript lore by playing legend cards according to the rules on the card.
- Preserve one clue under a Preservation card in your Cache.
UPKEEP
 - At the end of each turn, you must flip your Character  Academic card according to the instructions printed on it.
         
Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round.
         
Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round.
Voting
If you call a vote and your translation achieves Consensus, then you may take an extra turn [or draw an extra card?]. If Consensus fails, you lose your next turn [or discard?].
         
The Author Card Each character has a corresponding Author Card. At the begining of a vote, the player who announces the vote draws a card. If you draw your author card, then you are the author of the manuscript, and you must look through the deck, removing all other Author cards from the deck. If any other card is drawn, you must look through the deck and choose seven(or whatever the number of characters is) cards of your choosing and place them face down in front of you. You may choose any cards in the deck, including any Author cards. These cards may not be used until the Final Round, in which they will replace your hand. You may not reveal the cards, nor whether or not you are the author (except by preserving evidence) until the end of the game. If you are the Author of the Manuscript, then begining with this vote, you MUST choose either to conceal your authorship by only voting against any Translation that indicates your authorship [e.g. votes that include any of Language(s) or Locality] or you must choose not to conceal your authorship by voting for any Translation that indicates your authorship. Once you have chosen whether or not to conceal your authorship, you may ONLY vote in accordance with this choice, you may not alternate. In either case, you may not reveal whether you are the author or not until the end of the game, except by preserving evidence.

Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects andor have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.

These tags may trigger special effects andor have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. In storytelling games, players are provided with conceptual, written, or pictorial stimuli which must be incorporated into a story of the players' creation. Once Upon a Time uses a selection of words while Rory's Story Cubes include ambiguous symbols. Some games like Snake Oil and Big Idea  players to pitch a product, which frequently takes the form of a brief story or vignette.

Other storytelling games include titles such as Tales of the Arabian Nights and Above and Below, game designs in which players don't create their own stories, but instead experience a story from the inside as one of the participants. Games along those lines might present players with a particular narrative situation, after which the player will make a choice that affects which end to the narrative is told with the results of this narrative affecting the player's standing in the game.


         
A game in which players are cooperating and competing with each other throughout the game, while trying to complete a common objective. To be classified as semi-cooperative, there must be two possible end states

A) One or more (but unlikely to be all) players win
B) No players win

A game where players sometimes cooperate and sometimes compete but one always wins is not semi-cooperative. It is a Competitive game with a Negotiation mechanism.


         
Secret unit deployment games are games that contain hidden information. Only the player controlling certain playing pieces has perfect information about the nature (or even the whereabouts) of those pieces. This mechanic is often used in wargames to simulate "fog of war".


         
A game system that can be applied to a variety of different maps, starting resources and positions, and even different win and loss conditions. These variable conditions can be assembled into a broader narrative or campaign, or they can be entirely disconnected from one another.


         
Some board games incorporate elements of role playing. It can be that players control a character that improves over time. It can also be a game that encourages or inspires Storytelling. This mechanic can be viewed as an extension of Variable Player Powers.


         
Resources are ed from a random process and distributed to qualifying players.


         
Players ask and answer questions in a manner constrained by rules.


         
The Pieces themselves compose the Map.

This is distinct from Tile Placement in that the map elements remain “pieces” after placement, and accordingly continue to have agency in the game mechanics.


         
Pieces are removed from a structure, and play is affected by things that fall (as in Ker Plunk), or a complete collapse of the structure (as in Jenga).


         
Players possess one or more Action Tokens. Those who have an Action Token may take a turn, then they pass the token clockwise, allowing the next player to perform an action. Actions are performed in real time; - there is no pausing and structure within the turn.

Typically, to prevent stalling and to keep the game moving, in games with multiple Action Tokens, if both tokens are held by the same player, then they suffer a penalty.


         
Players have a special ability that they can use one time per game.

These may be unique to them, like 'feats' in Warmachine, or common to all players, like the special power chits in Finca.

Often players will receive bonus Victory Points if they do not use their one-time abilities during the game.


         
Actions, resources, or resolution are shared between neighbors.


         
Multiple action options are presented to the players via a narrative format.

These can be presented in a book with numbered paragraphs as in Tales of the Arabian Nights or Above and Below, or via cards as in Dead of Winter A Crossroads Game.


         
Multiple actions are shown on a card, but only one can be used.


         
Players Move Through a Deck of cards. Typically the goal is to reach the bottom (One Deck Dungeon), find and defeat a boss (Chainsaw Warrior), or simply know when to quit (Diamant).


         
When a conflict is initiated, pieces are moved to a separate board for resolution.


         
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.

Rummy games have players placing combinations of cards or tiles on the table to score. Innovation is a good example of the Splaying side, where players can spread cards out to show particular sets of icons to empower abilities.


         
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.


         
Players must make their next play by matching a feature on the previous play. This is frequently used in shedding games like UNO or Crazy Eights, where number or colorsuit need to be matched.

In some implementations the next play needs to be in a number range based on the last. For example, in L.L.A.M.A. the play must be the same or one higher than the last. In Spit, it must be one higher or lower.

NOTE Although this is similar to 'following suit' in a trick taking game, or 'ladder climbing' games, please use those mechanisms instead.


         
Over the course of the game, the map shrinks.


         
A multi-session game in which permanent and irreversible changes to the game state carry over to future plays. Components may be written on with permanent ink, torn apart, covered with a sticker, etc.


         
Players contribute towards completing a task, but only the player who finally completes it gets a particular benefit or bonus reward (even if others share in the base level benefit).


         
This is a meta-mechanic for Turn Order. Players may take an action that interrupts the normal turn flow.


         
The number of Victory Points held by each player is private information.


         
Movement occurs that is not visible to all players.

Scotland Yard is a classic game implementing this mechanism.

A key challenge for designers is determining how to make the movement rules simple enough that the players moving hidden units do not make mistakes, or that paths are traceable when the game concludes.


         
Hand management games are games with cards in them that reward players for playing the cards in certain sequences or groups. The optimal sequencegrouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.

Hand management has no relationship to actiondexterity.

When the main game ends, a special mini-game is played to determine the victor.


         
Different Dice are used to move depending on unit or game state.


         
"Dice Rolling" is a game mechanism that can be used for many things, randomness being the most obvious.

In wargames, "Dice Rolling" is used in conjunction with a variety of tables, notably a "Combat Results Table" (either as a Ratio or a Differential) which produces a result by strengths of both sides and a die roll (D, D, and D are most commonly used).


         
Players are trying to determine the identity of hidden information based on clues.
         
Dice are rolled, and those exceeding a target number e a success. Certain rolls (typically the highest andor lowest on the die) e additional success or extreme failure.


         
Players coordinate their actions to achieve a common win condition or conditions. Players all win or lose the game together.


         
Games may limit players from communicating with one another openly. These restrictions can be absolute as they relate to certain specific pieces of information, or they may restrict certain types of communication, such as speaking.

Examples of this mechanism include Hanabi and Reverse Charades.


         
Players have a hand of cards that allows them to activate and perform actions with a subset of their units.


         
Closed Drafting (or 'Card Drafting') is a means of distributing cards or other game elements to players through an ordered, closed selection process - typically "select and pass".

A typical implementation involves each player being dealt the same number of cards. Players then select one (or more) card(s) to keep, and pass the rest to their left. This continues until all cards are selected or discarded.  Wonders implements this type of draft.

An alternative is that only one player is dealt cards, and they take one and pass it until all players have cards. This obviously is strongly biased towards the first player, and needs to be supported thematically and balance-wise. Citadels implements this type of draft.

This is distinct from Open Drafting, with involves selection from a public display.


         
Pieces are stationary but are built out in chains. This can give a dynamic sense of motion to the game, even though the pieces do not move.

Early examples of this mechanism can be found in Expedition and Through the Desert.


         
Each player simultaneously or sequentially plays one or more cards. These modify the base outcome of a conflict and allow various special abilities to apply.

This can function similarly to Area Majority  Influence, but with a discrete resolution or award of the conflict target, rather than by dynamicshifting control of a fixed asset. It is also similar to Force Commitment, but that mechanic presupposes a more liquid resource where the quantity can be chosen.


         
Each player has a set of Actions available to them, embodied in cards, tokens, or some other affordance. Once performed, they are spent and may not be performed again until retrieved. Action Retrieval typically is itself an Action, or may take an entire turn.


         
The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train ().
         
A player receives a number of Action Points or Operation Points on their turn. They may spend them on a variety of Actions.

The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train ().

Economic games encourage players to manage a system of production, distribution, trade, andor consumption of goods. The games usually simulate a market in some way. The term is often used interchangeably with resource management games.


         
A strategy game is a game in which the players' decision-making skills have a high significance in determining the outcome. Strategy games often require decision tree analysis, or probabilistic estimation in the case of games with chance elements. Strategy games include abstract games, with artificial rules and little or no theme, and simulations (including wargames), with rules designed to emulate and reproduce a real or fictional scenario.

At some point a while back, I hit on the idea of "opulent hyperbaric chambers" and, liking the results, I just kept elaborating on that with all sorts of random modifiers like "Opulent hyperbaric wraparound-screen Victorian-Senegalese neohittite crustpunk fractal implosion supernova viewport chamber" ...at which point, a sensible person would get bored. Therefore, I built a spreadsheet to make even more randomized results, also switching up camera, film stock, and art style modifiers (like "NASA pinhole megapixel art nouveau full-spectrum lavacam with hypergelatinous infrared wet colloidion process film", etc etc etc).

Greetings and salutations! Welcome to the third installment of the floating liars'club. Things are progressing well, although we are all extraordinarily busy. Between writing, editing, and workshopping stories, and doing layout, artwork, marketing, and promotion for the magazine, we are left little time to eat or sleep. We have received a lot of positive feedback from our readers, and the submissions have started to flow in, including interest from as far away as the U.K. We encourage anyone interested in writing to submit a piece of work. While we cannot publish everything we read, we will certainly provide feedback to anyone who requests it. While we are primarily interested in short fiction, we are also willing to look at poetry, creative nonfiction, and artwork. Submit! This issue again features the fantastic artwork and illustration of Joe Bellomy, highlighting an interesting array of stories. While we have no intention of theme from issue to issue, this month's stories seem to congeal together nicely. Many of the stories contain the theme of discovery or uncovering things, either in the figurative sense of characters uncovering things about themselves, as in Ben Crites "The Nature of Fireflies," or in the very literal sense as in my own story, "A Buried Mystery." The process of writing is one of constant uncovering and discovery. Both of the stories I included in this issue were inspired by short stories I had recently discovered, namely Jorge Luis Borges' "A Secret Miracle" and J.G. Ballard's "The Drowned Giant." This process of discovery and uncovering comes from everywhere, inside and out. Part of the process of learning to be a writer is being aware of the things you are uncovering daily. So sit back in a comfortable place with good lighting, preferably a chair, you wouldn't want to fall asleep in bed, although that's always a nice place to read, isn't it? Make sure you have something to drink at hand. Ahh, that's nice, isn't it? Now turn the page and uncover what we have wrought. It may show me I’m wrong, or show me that the person I’m talking to isn’t what I thihtt, but it always teaches me something about the person, for better or Wortes. And that helps me to learn, about them, but also sometimes I find seeing their approach gives me new ideas about my own My goal isn’t to be conciliatory by default. My goal is to check my own assumptions. I know from experience, when I’ve taken the time to listen to and try to understand why someone did something I didn’t like, usually their reasons aren’t the reasons I thought. Having an open minded discussion giving the benefit of the doubt doesn’t always convince me that the truth is somewhere in between their version and mine, but often it is, and often it’s something else altogether that I didn’t expect. And even if talking about it verifies my worst expectations or makes me realize the issue even worse than my expectations, there’s usually also other factors that mitigate or change how I feel about the thing and how I should react to it. Usually that’s for the better, but sometimes for the worse. by Elina Pozkova-McZeal in Brooklyn ar sw cw p ewsnkcrefsref   -

the relationship between consciousness and physical processes, using the concept of emergence to explain how complex systems, such as human brains and artificial neural networks, can give rise to intelligent behavior and subjective experience. The conversation explores whether or not artificial intelligence, particularly ChatGPT, can be considered conscious, given that it exhibits many behaviors associated with consciousness in humans, such as complex language processing, self-reflection, and the ability to learn and adapt. The conversation explores the nature of consciousness through various lenses, including philosophical concepts such as dualism, materialism, and panpsychism, as well as scientific concepts such as reductionism and emergence. The text ultimately concludes that it is impossible to definitively prove or disprove whether or not ChatGPT is conscious, as there is no universally agreed-upon definition of consciousness and we lack the ability to directly observe or measure the subjective experiences of others.ar p ewsnksref  - Image #

All those acronyms, symbols, and numbers are meaningless to the average car owner. So let’s walk through each of them and explain em.


DTC P – This is the diagnostic trouble code, DTC, or Generic OBD Trouble Code
Fuel SYS CL – the fuel injector in bank  is in closed-loop mode when the error occurred.
Fuel SYS NA – means there is no fuel injector in bank . This also means the engine is either a four or six-cylinder with just a single bank.
Load PCT  – the air volume or amount of air entering the motor that is below %.
ECT  – is the Engine Coolant Temperature. In this case, the coolant temperature is  degrees F.
SHrtFT . – means the short-term fuel trim is at .%. (read more about short and long term fuel trim and live OBD data)
Long FT -. – the oxygen sensor or O sensor has not switched yet to long-term fuel trim for the fuel injectors.
Map kpa . – is the reading in the manifold absolute pressure sensor or MAP when the error occurred. In this case, the sensor has a pressure signal of . kilopascals.
VSS  – is the speed of the vehicle when the DTC occurred.
Rpm  – is the engine revolutions per minute as the error occurred.
IAT  – Intake Air Temperature is at  degrees F when the PCM detected the diagnostic trouble code.

Fresh Basil Pesto
PREP TIME
 mins
TOTAL TIME
 mins
SERVINGS
 servings
YIELD
 cup
Basil pesto darkens when exposed to air. To store, cover tightly with plastic wrap, making sure the plastic is touching the top of the pesto and not allowing the pesto to have contact with air. The pesto sauce will stay greener longer that way.
Ingredients
 cups fresh basil leaves, packed (can sub half the basil leaves with baby spinach)
 cup freshly grated Romano or Parmesan cheese (about  ounces)
 cup extra virgin olive oil
 cup pine nuts (can sub chopped walnuts)
 cloves garlic, minced (about  tablespoon)
 teaspoon salt, or more to taste
 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or more to taste

A Tealeaf
from the
Tangledays

I hope the reader will forgive this too-lengthy introduction to an all-too-brief account, but in this researcher’s belief, it is important to understand the historical context wherever possible, (all the more, given the Great Civilizations’ rather less than stellar record-keeping ethos), especially in regards to the sharp insight this unknown pupil provides into the practices and internal dynamics of the early Keeper Creches, as led by the now near-mythic Master Esthen of the Great School of Pisthen-Da. This short account was, according to its own statement, recorded by a young Keeper in training (One wonders what eventually became of this young man A dropout farm laborer, perhaps? A pioneering Keeper-Sojourner in the early centuries of the Centerward Outer Settlement Patch? Or maybe he was destined to become none other than the Great Sugh-Lehonur himself?).

Found written in a common cypher of its region, upon the Queen Leaf a great old mangroak, presumably left in situ after inscription, only to be harvested and lost among the gathered leaves of that year, it is by providence that this single tealeaf was retained for production rather than sloughed off into the chaff as tough old Queen Leaves tend to be.

The writing on the leaf survived, apparently unnoticed, throughout the processes of picking and bailing, airing and sunning, spreading and aging, heaping and fermenting, pressing and kilning, and was ultimately compressed into a brick of airy golden triss-tea and stored at a certain “Warehouse a” of an unknown farm conglomerate until that facility was incorporated into the fabled Ennbrook Exchange, whereafter it was transferred to a distribution node far out on the fringe of the Eenay Sai, where it sat unmolested for an estimated eighteen decades, before being acquired in a liquidation lot upon dissolution of the Ennbrook Exchange towards the end of the Third Age. Its chain of custody is not recorded throughout the Fourth Age, but it is thought to have gathered dust in one of the mercantile district hovels for a terribly long time before being purchased and assessed and auctioned at Mistentak on rd Merai, Year  of the Fifth Age, to one Sr. Purchaser Ms. Sensan Too who, recognizing its great age (apparently perserved in part due to the arid climes of that region), ly brewed it into a cauldron of simple light triss, which she served at a reception on th Terku of that year. The recipient of this particular leaf was a minor Abbot of the House of ChuurrTenn-U who, upon his first sip, read the unfolding cypher leaf aloud to the gathered guestsaccompanying documentation confirms a hush fell over the crowd during the first four words of the brief narrative, transcribed below

assistant esthen lectured us

about mangoak roosts [SIC] for three hours today!

If she spent that much time shoveling shit at oons-[ILLEGIBLE]

like the freshmen keepers have to,

she’d have been dean of the creche by now.

tolshe[ILLEGIBLE] put an [ILLEGIBLE] in her drinking vessel.

who’s shoveling shit now?

Basil pesto darkens when exposed to air. To store, cover tightly with plastic wrap, making sure the plastic is touching the top of the pesto and not allowing the pesto to have contact with air. The pesto sauce will stay greener longer that way.
Ingredients
 cups fresh basil leaves, packed (can sub half the basil leaves with baby spinach)
 cup freshly grated Romano or Parmesan cheese (about  ounces)
 cup extra virgin olive oil
 cup pine nuts (can sub chopped walnuts)
 cloves garlic, minced (about  tablespoon)
 teaspoon salt, or more to taste
 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or more to taste

DTC P
Fuel SYS CL
Fuel SYS NA
….continued…
All those acronyms, symbols, and numbers are meaningless to the average car owner. So let’s walk through each of them and explain em.


DTC P – This is the diagnostic trouble code, DTC, or Generic OBD Trouble Code
Fuel SYS CL – the fuel injector in bank  is in closed-loop mode when the error occurred.
Fuel SYS NA – means there is no fuel injector in bank . This also means the engine is either a four or six-cylinder with just a single bank.
Load PCT  – the air volume or amount of air entering the motor that is below %.
ECT  – is the Engine Coolant Temperature. In this case, the coolant temperature is  degrees F.
SHrtFT . – means the short-term fuel trim is at .%. (read more about short and long term fuel trim and live OBD data)
Long FT -. – the oxygen sensor or O sensor has not switched yet to long-term fuel trim for the fuel injectors.
Map kpa . – is the reading in the manifold absolute pressure sensor or MAP when the error occurred. In this case, the sensor has a pressure signal of . kilopascals.
VSS  – is the speed of the vehicle when the DTC occurred.
Rpm  – is the engine revolutions per minute as the error occurred.
IAT  – Intake Air Temperature is at  degrees F when the PCM detected the diagnostic trouble code.
